name: Nandrolone phenylpropionate

card.summary: A short-ester injectable anabolic steroid (Durabolin) used medically for muscle wasting and by bodybuilders to build lean mass.
card.note: Controlled substance in many countries; non-medical use is illicit.

quick.overview:
Nandrolone phenylpropionate (NPP) is a short-acting ester of nandrolone, an anabolic-androgenic steroid. It was sold as Durabolin and used medically for catabolic states such as burns and wasting.

Bodybuilders and physique athletes report using it to gain muscle and recover from hard training, which is the appearance connection. Clinical research is mostly medical and dated, not about physique outcomes [1][2].
quick.how: In bodybuilding communities NPP is described as an injectable oil, valued for a shorter active window than nandrolone decanoate. Details of use are not given here.
quick.risks: Nandrolone esters are controlled substances in many countries, including Schedule III in the US and Class C in the UK. Reported effects include acne, increased hair growth, suppressed natural testosterone and, at high doses, cardiovascular and fertility effects [1].

lead: Nandrolone phenylpropionate (NPP, brand name Durabolin) is the phenylpropionate ester of nandrolone, or 19-nortestosterone, an anabolic-androgenic steroid. Bodybuilders, powerlifters and other physique athletes use nandrolone esters to build lean muscle and to recover from hard training, which is the route by which it affects appearance: more muscle mass and fuller, denser muscle on the frame. Wikipedia describes nandrolone esters as among the most popular anabolic steroids in bodybuilding and sport and attributes this to a favourable anabolic-to-androgenic ratio with comparatively weak androgenic and estrogenic effects.[1][7]

Medically, nandrolone esters have been used for anaemias, wasting and catabolic states such as burns, cancer and AIDS, osteoporosis and breast cancer, with reported effects on muscle, appetite, red blood cells and bone.[1][7][8] Nandrolone was first synthesised in 1950, NPP was described in 1957 and introduced for medical use in 1959, and nandrolone decanoate followed in 1962; NPP is now scarcely available as a pharmaceutical.[1][7] It is the shorter-acting of the two common esters, with an intramuscular elimination half-life of about 2.7 days and a duration of about 5 to 7 days.[7]

Nandrolone esters are controlled substances in many countries, including Schedule III in the United States and Class C in the United Kingdom, so non-medical use is generally illicit.[1][7] Published research on NPP itself is mostly older clinical trials and animal work; the more recent human trials concern nandrolone decanoate and medical populations, and none of these studies measured physique outcomes in healthy lifters.[2][3][4][5][6][10][11]

paras: Bodybuilders, powerlifters and other athletes use nandrolone for muscle and performance, and Wikipedia lists nandrolone esters among the most widely used steroids for physique and performance enhancement worldwide.[1][7] Within the bodybuilding community, NPP is described as an injectable oil prized for its shorter active window compared with nandrolone decanoate; details of use are not given here.[7] The steroid has been banned at the Olympics since 1974.[1]

Nandrolone esters, mainly decanoate and less commonly phenylpropionate, have been used for anaemias, cachexia, osteoporosis and breast cancer, and Wikipedia says they are used increasingly rarely for catabolic states such as major burns, cancer and AIDS.[1] NPP is described as used mainly for advanced breast cancer in women and as adjunct therapy for postmenopausal or senile osteoporosis; historically it had other uses, and from the 1970s its use became more restricted.[7] For nandrolone decanoate, Wikipedia reports US approval for anaemia of chronic kidney disease and UK approval for postmenopausal osteoporosis, with off-label use for lean-mass preservation in HIV and wasting syndromes.[8]

NPP is a prodrug of nandrolone, which is an androgen receptor agonist with strong anabolic effects and weak androgenic effects relative to testosterone; in rodents the anabolic-to-androgenic ratio is roughly 1:3 to 1:16, and nandrolone binds the human androgen receptor with higher relative affinity than testosterone.[7] Anabolic steroids in general are said to raise protein synthesis, reduce muscle breakdown possibly by opposing glucocorticoids, and favour differentiation of precursor cells toward muscle rather than fat storage.[9]

Nandrolone is also a progestogen, with about 20 percent of progesterone's receptor affinity, and has low estrogenic activity, mainly through its metabolite estradiol; like other anabolic steroids it suppresses gonadotropins.[1][7] It is converted by 5-alpha-reductase to the much weaker 5-alpha-dihydronandrolone, so it is less potentiated in skin, scalp and prostate than testosterone, and 5-alpha-reductase inhibitors such as finasteride can increase its androgenic effects unlike most other anabolic steroids.[1][7]

NPP is hydrolysed to nandrolone in the blood and reduced in the liver; nandrolone's own half-life is under 4.3 hours, while the intramuscular NPP elimination half-life is about 2.7 days and the duration about 5 to 7 days, much shorter than for nandrolone decanoate (about 2 to 3 weeks).[1][7] Metabolites include 5-alpha-dihydronandrolone, 19-norandrosterone and 19-noretiocholanolone, excreted mainly in urine.[7] A 1997 study in healthy men followed plasma nandrolone, testosterone and inhibin for 32 days after a single intramuscular injection of nandrolone esters, examining effects of ester, injection site and injection volume.[3]

NPP (C27H34O3, molar mass about 406.6 g/mol) is a synthetic estrane steroid, the C17-beta phenylpropionate ester of nandrolone, which is testosterone lacking the C19 methyl group. It is also known as nandrolone phenpropionate and nandrolone hydrocinnamate.[7] Nandrolone is made by routes that rely on the Birch reduction.[1]

Reported effects of nandrolone include acne, increased hair growth and voice deepening, with virilisation in women described as less pronounced than with most other anabolic steroids and uncommon at recommended doses, but more likely with higher doses or long-term use.[1][7] High doses may cause cardiovascular toxicity, hypogonadism and infertility, and scalp hair loss is described as theoretical.[1] For nandrolone decanoate, Wikipedia adds fluid retention, reduced sperm production, testicular atrophy, gynaecomastia and changes in cholesterol and blood pressure, and states that, unlike 17-alpha-alkylated steroids, it is not linked to liver toxicity.[8]

Anabolic steroids as a class have been associated in published reviews with aggression and mood effects and, in one cited kidney study, focal segmental glomerulosclerosis; the International Agency for Research on Cancer lists them as probably carcinogenic to humans (Group 2A).[9] In a 2025 meta-analysis of nandrolone in postmenopausal osteoporosis, nandrolone was associated with more mostly mild virilising adverse events.[11]

NPP is a Schedule III controlled substance in the United States, Schedule IV in Canada, Class C in the United Kingdom and prescription-only in Australia, and is generally illicit for non-medical use where controlled.[7] The IOC urinary threshold for the metabolite 19-norandrosterone is 2.0 micrograms per litre, and Wikipedia reports that in a study of 621 athletes at the 1998 Nagano Games none exceeded 0.4 micrograms per litre.[1] Nandrolone doping cases in the late 1990s and 2000s are documented, including those of Linford Christie, Dieter Baumann and Merlene Ottey in 1999, Mark Richardson, whose case highlighted detection-method false positives, and C. J. Hunter, who said lysine caused his positive test and in 2004 told a grand jury he had injected nandrolone; Marion Jones admitted to using the drug in October 2007.[1] Trace 19-norandrosterone was also found as a contaminant in androstenedione supplements sold in the US until 2004.[1]

No clinical studies of NPP for physique or muscle-building in healthy people were found. Human research is medical. A 1990 randomised trial in 183 abdominal-surgery patients included one group receiving nebulised heparin plus a single NPP injection to examine postoperative deep vein thrombosis.[4] A 1971 clinical study and a 1974 trial examined the drug's effect on bone-marrow suppression caused by cyclophosphamide,[5][12] and a 1975 South African trial compared Masteril with Durabolin in breast cancer.[6] A Cochrane review of pharmacotherapy for patellofemoral pain lists anabolic steroids among options considered.[2]

More recent trials concern nandrolone decanoate. A 2026 systematic review and meta-analysis of 15 randomised trials in adults with chronic kidney disease reported a lean body mass increase of about 2.6 kg in 4 trials (n = 125), with haemoglobin and haematocrit favouring nandrolone, though heterogeneity was high, certainty very low and long-term safety data sparse.[10] A 2025 meta-analysis of seven randomised trials (293 participants) in postmenopausal osteoporosis reported reduced fracture risk, modest bone density gains, less pain and more muscle mass, with more mild virilising events.[11] A 2025 single-centre prospective study of 100 postmenopausal women given nandrolone with oral alendronate for 12 months reported improved bone density and a rise in lean body mass without a control group.[13]

Early animal studies examined NPP's metabolic and growth effects, including protein metabolism in rats (1985) and craniofacial growth in rats (1994), and a 1995 study reported that an anabolic-androgenic steroid increased running endurance in rats; a 1993 review covered the metabolic effects of anabolic steroids.[14][15][16][17] A 2025 mouse study of nandrolone decanoate during a volume-overload training week reported that no nandrolone-treated mice became fatigued, versus four of the sham group, with lower TNF-alpha and oxidative stress; these are animal results.[18]

timeline.event: NPP is introduced for medical use as Durabolin.[1][7]
Nandrolone decanoate is introduced as the next nandrolone ester.[8]
Medical use of NPP becomes more restricted, mainly to breast cancer and osteoporosis in women.[7]
Nandrolone is banned at the Olympics.[1]
Nandrolone doping cases involve Linford Christie, Dieter Baumann and Merlene Ottey.[1]
Marion Jones admits to using nandrolone.[1]

lore.intro: Reference material describes nandrolone esters as popular in bodybuilding, and the claims below summarise how that popularity is explained.[1][7]

claims.claim: Nandrolone gives strong muscle-building effects with milder androgenic side effects than testosterone.
claims.believers: Wikipedia attributes the popularity of nandrolone esters in bodybuilding to the favourable anabolic-to-androgenic ratio and weaker androgenic and estrogenic effects.[1][7]
claims.experts: Pharmacology references report that 5-alpha-reductase converts nandrolone to a weaker androgen, reducing effects in skin, scalp and prostate, but note virilisation still occurs at higher doses or with long-term use.[1][7]

claims.claim: NPP's short duration makes it easier to manage than nandrolone decanoate.
claims.believers: Bodybuilding descriptions value NPP's shorter active window compared with decanoate.[7]
claims.experts: The pharmacokinetic figures (half-life about 2.7 days, duration 5 to 7 days versus 2 to 3 weeks for decanoate) are documented, though no study compares the two for physique outcomes.[1][7]

claims.claim: Nandrolone is safer for hair than other steroids.
claims.believers: The drug's conversion to a weak metabolite is cited as lowering effects on scalp and prostate.[7]
claims.experts: Wikipedia calls scalp hair loss a theoretical possibility and says 5-alpha-reductase inhibitors such as finasteride can increase nandrolone's androgenic effects.[1][7]

claims.claim: Nandrolone improves muscle and strength in medical populations.
claims.believers: Clinicians have used it for wasting and anaemia.[1]
claims.experts: A 2026 meta-analysis found about 2.6 kg lean mass gain in CKD trials but very low certainty, and a 2025 meta-analysis in osteoporosis reported more muscle mass with moderate certainty.[10][11]

claims.claim: Nandrolone use cannot be detected or is excused by contaminated supplements.
claims.believers: Some athletes have attributed positive tests to supplements such as lysine.[1]
claims.experts: The IOC threshold for 19-norandrosterone is 2.0 micrograms per litre; trace contamination was found in androstenedione supplements, and one athlete later admitted injecting nandrolone.[1]

claims.claim: Anabolic steroid use carries long-term health risks.
claims.believers: Users acknowledge side effects such as acne, hair growth and hormonal suppression.[1]
claims.experts: Reviews associate anabolic steroids with mood, kidney and cardiovascular effects, and IARC lists them as probably carcinogenic (Group 2A).[8][9]
